vignette:
The first thing I noticed about Mr. Achebe was how carefully he chose his seat. He settled into the chair in my office with a slow, deliberate motion, his back straight, his hands resting flat on his knees. He is a tall man, seventy-eight years old, with silver hair and the deliberate, measured speech of a lifetime spent among books. He wore a cardigan, even though the room was warm. He told me, without being asked, that he had been a librarian for forty-two years, retired now, but that he still went to the main branch three times a week to help with the archives. “It keeps the mind orderly,” he said. “A place for everything.”

He came to see me at his wife’s urging. For the last three years, he has been waking up at 2:47 in the morning. He does not need to look at a clock. He knows the time by the quality of the dark. He lies there, his body rigid, listening. He hears nothing but the sound of his own blood moving in his ears, but his body is convinced that something is about to happen. He waits for it. The wait can last an hour, sometimes two.

This is what happened.

On a Saturday afternoon in 2015, Mr. Achebe was at the central market in his home city of Jos, Nigeria. He was buying yams. He remembers the exact weight of the yam in his hand, the rough brown skin against his palm. He remembers the sun was hot. He remembers a woman in a yellow headscarf laughing at a joke he could not hear. Then there was a sound he still cannot describe as an explosion, because the word is too small. It was a physical event—a punch of air and pressure that threw him forward onto his knees. The yam rolled away. The laughing woman was gone. There was dust, and a high, thin ringing, and then the screaming began.

He did not run. He stayed on his knees for what felt like a very long time. He remembers thinking, very clearly, *I must not move until I know where the pieces are.* He does not know what he meant by “pieces.” He does not tell me this part easily. He was not physically hurt, but his ears bled for three days.

He came to the United States two years later, to live with his son in a quiet suburb. He was grateful. He was safe. But safety, he has learned, is not a place you can find on a map.

He cannot go to the grocery store on a Saturday. The crowds, the noise, the way people bump into him without apologizing—it makes his heart race until he feels like he is choking. He goes on Tuesday mornings, at 7:00 AM, when the store is empty. He has memorized the layout. He walks the same path every time. If a display has been moved, he leaves without buying anything.

He does not like the word “terrorism.” He says it sounds like something from the news, something that happens to other people. What happened to him was a Tuesday. It was a market. It was a yam in his hand. He does not watch the news. He cannot stand the sound of sirens. He has stopped reading the newspapers he spent his life organizing. His wife, Grace, has to check the mail first, because if she is not there, he will let the envelopes pile up for weeks. He is afraid of what might be inside.

He is not afraid of dying. He told me this, and I believe him. He is afraid of the moment before. He is afraid of the stillness that comes just before the air breaks. He is afraid of the waiting.

He sits in my office, straight-backed, hands on his knees. He is not a man who cries. But when he talks about the yam, about the way it rolled away from him, his voice drops to a whisper. “I should have held on to it,” he says. “I should have held on.”
